title: Deal Psychology & Technical Arguments for Platform Owners
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook helps account teams and solutions architects influence platform owners (platform engineering, data teams, infra leads) by combining behavioral framing (deal psychology) with concise technical arguments and evidence. It is written for customer-facing teams who must navigate procurement, security, and engineering objections while accelerating to a pilot that proves cost and latency benefits.

Audience
- Primary: Platform owners (VP/Director of Platform, Principal Engineers)
- Secondary: Procurement, Security (CISO/engineering security), Head of ML/AI

Executive positioning (one-paragraph elevator)
Redwood Inference provides a unified runtime that reduces per-token inference cost through adaptive batching, KV/prefix caching, and workload-aware quantization while keeping latency SLOs predictable. For platform owners, the value is predictable unit economics, lower operational debt compared to bespoke stacks, and a single API/ops surface that reduces maintenance and supports hybrid deployment (hosted, dedicated, private VPC).

Top 4 platform-first message pillars (talking points mapped to objections)
1) Predictable economics (Objection: "We can't forecast costs")
   - Message: Reserved capacity and per-route token breakdowns let teams model spend to the hour.
   - Evidence: Dedicated commit with 95th percentile token rate smoothing, token-level billing export to BigQuery.
   - Quick script: "We can run a 30-day collector to produce a per-route cost curve and forecast budget impact with +/-10% accuracy."

2) Interoperability and escape hatches (Objection: "We don't want vendor lock-in")
   - Message: Same API semantics across hosted/dedicated/private; model pinning and portable model artifacts reduce migration lift.
   - Evidence: ONNX/torchscript-compatible packaging and model manifest that maps to runtime config.

3) Operational consolidation (Objection: "Maintaining another system is risky")
   - Message: One telemetry plane, role-based access controls, and incident runbooks shorten mean-time-to-detect/repair.
   - Evidence: Console dashboards, token-level tracing, and SLO templates for model endpoints (example SLO: 99th percentile generation latency <250ms for 1k token targets).

4) Security & compliance alignment (Objection: "How do we keep data in our control?")
   - Message: Private deployment model with customer-managed VPC and KMS integration; audit logs exported to customer SIEM.
   - Evidence: HSM/KMS key wrap support, TLS mTLS, and retention policy controls.

Competitive snapshot (quick reference)
- Primary competitors: Managed endpoint players and cloud ML services.
- Differentiators to highlight:
  - Unified runtime across deployment models (avoid conversation fragmentation).
  - Cost levers visible in console (batching/caching/quantization) with suggested presets for workloads.
  - Rollout primitives (canary, A/B, automatic fallback to smaller quantized model on resource pressure).

Short competitor cheat-sheet (talking bullets to use in meetings)
- Competitor A (managed endpoints): Good for one-off experiments, poor for multi-tenant cost predictability. Emphasize Redwood's commitment and dedicated pools for predictability.
- Competitor B (self-hosted runtime open source): Strong control but high ops burden; emphasize Redwood's managed private option and runbooks that reduce internal effort.
- Cloud ML feature set: Integrated with broad infra but often lacking model-serving-level cache/batching and token-level billing—call these out when customers worry about chargeback.

Pricing framing and pilot packaging (step-by-step)
1) Discovery (2 weeks)
   - Action: Collect representative traffic (sample logs, traffic distribution, prompt sizes).
   - Artifacts delivered: Traffic histogram, cost forecast (hosted vs dedicated vs private), recommended pilot config.

2) Pilot (30–60 days)
   - Baseline: Instrument 7–14 days of live traffic to capture P95 latency and token distribution.
   - Pilot config: Dedicated small pool (4–8 GPUs) OR private single-node VM + NLB with canary route (5% traffic).
   - Success criteria (customer-defined):
     - Cost: >=20% reduction in per-token cost vs current ops (or unit cost target met).
     - Latency: P95 generation latency within 1.25x of baseline application requirement.
     - Reliability: No unhandled degradation for 99.5% of requests during pilot window.

3) Commit & Scale
   - Convert pilot results into a committed capacity contract or private deployment plan.

Pricing examples (plain JSON you can paste into a discovery note)
{
  "pilot_duration_days": "45",
  "pilot_capacity": "4x-A100-equivalent",
  "baseline_cost_estimate_usd_month": "18,000",
  "redwood_estimated_usd_month": "13,500",
  "estimated_savings_pct": "25%"
}

Handling common technical objections (scripted responses)
- "We have bursty traffic at month-end": Recommend autoscaling burst capacity + warm pools for critical routes; show historical tail behavior from similar customers (median warm-up 90s for a cold pool).
- "We require model explainability": Point to structured output and function/tool-calling features; offer to run a sample eval and produce token-level diff logs.
- "We can't send production data out": Offer Private deployment with customer KMS and optional data-path restrictions; include an NDA and data handling annex in pilot contract.

Security FAQ for platform owners (concise answers to reduce friction)
Q: Can we use our KMS/HSM?
A: Yes — we integrate with customer KMS providers for key wrapping. For on-prem HSMs we provide a connector using PKCS#11 where required.

Q: How are access controls enforced?
A: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) scoped to token routes, model versions, and audit exports. Console and API keys support token scoping by route and environment.

Q: What is retained in logs?
A: Only metadata by default (latency, tokens, model version). Customer can opt-in to request/response logging; retention and redaction rules are configurable per-project.

Q: Do you support SOC2/ISO evidence?
A: Yes — Redwood maintains SOC2 Type II and can provide evidence packages for enterprise diligence. For pilot requests, provide our security questionnaire and we will start the evidence exchange.

Proof points and short case study vignettes (for field use)
- Financial services analytics platform: Reduced inference bill by 28% after a three-week quantization and caching optimization; moved from prototype to dedicated pool in 45 days.
- Customer success platform: Improved median response time from 420ms to 210ms for common 256-token prompts by enabling KV caching and smaller quantized model for non-critical routes.

Playbook: How to run the “Platform Owner Pilot” (step-by-step checklist)
1) Pre-kickoff (owner: AE/SE)
   - Collect traffic sample (s3/CSV) and key prompts.
   - Email security questionnaire and pilot NDA to customer.
2) Kickoff (owner: SE + Customer Platform Lead)
   - Share success criteria and measurement plan.
   - Provision pilot env (hosted ephemeral or private sandbox).
3) Instrumentation (owner: SE)
   - Enable token-level export to customer BigQuery/S3.
   - Add tracing headers for per-request attribution.
4) Run (owner: SE/Customer)
   - Live run for 30–60 days, weekly check-ins.
   - If errors exceed 0.5% of requests, trigger mitigation playbook.
5) Close (owner: AE/SE)
   - Deliver final ROI report and deployment recommendation.

Ownership and escalation
- Pilot owner: Solutions Engineering (SE)
- Security lead: Security Engagement Team (SEC)
